content: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by T-cell-mediated inflammation and demyelination within the central nervous system. The disease course is unpredictable, and current therapeutic strategies aim to manage relapses, prevent disease progression, and minimize disability. However, no treatment currently exists that can achieve these goals both safely and effectively. Alemtuzumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody, has shown promise in clinical trials as a potential treatment for MS. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and risks of alemtuzumab, either as a standalone therapy or in combination with other treatments, for individuals with any form of MS. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared alemtuzumab to placebo, other active drugs, or different doses, regimens, or durations of alemtuzumab. The primary outcomes evaluated were relapse-free survival, sustained disease progression-free survival, and the proportion of participants experiencing at least one adverse event. Secondary outcomes included clinical disability-free status, quality of life, changes in disability, fatigue, new or enlarging lesions on MRI, and dropout rates. Three RCTs involving 1,713 participants were included in the analysis. These trials compared intravenous alemtuzumab to subcutaneous interferon beta-1a in individuals with relapsing-remitting MS. Participants were either treatment-naive or had experienced at least one relapse after prior treatment with interferon or glatiramer acetate. Alemtuzumab was administered at doses of 12 mg/day or 24 mg/day for five consecutive days at baseline and again at 12 months, or at 24 mg/day for three days at 12 and 24 months. The interferon beta-1a group received 44 μg three times weekly. For alemtuzumab at a dose of 12 mg/day: 1. It may improve relapse-free survival at 36 months (hazard ratio [HR] 0.31, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.18 to 0.53; low-certainty evidence). 2. It may improve sustained disease progression-free survival at 36 months (HR 0.25, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.56; low-certainty evidence). 3. It may have little to no effect on the proportion of participants experiencing at least one adverse event at 36 months (risk ratio [RR] 1.00, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.02; low-certainty evidence), although the overall rate of adverse events was high in both treatment groups. 4. It may slightly reduce disability at 36 months (mean difference [MD] −0.70, 95% CI −1.04 to −0.36; low-certainty evidence). 5. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the risk of dropouts at 36 months (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.14; very low-certainty evidence). For alemtuzumab at a dose of 24 mg/day: 1. It may improve relapse-free survival at 36 months (HR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40; low-certainty evidence). 2. It may improve sustained disease progression-free survival at 36 months (HR 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.69; low-certainty evidence). 3. It may have little to no effect on the proportion of participants experiencing at least one adverse event at 36 months (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.02; low-certainty evidence), although the overall rate of adverse events was high in both treatment groups. 4. It may slightly reduce disability at 36 months (MD −0.83, 95% CI −1.16 to −0.50; low-certainty evidence). 5. It may reduce the risk of dropouts at 36 months (RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.57; low-certainty evidence). The studies did not consistently evaluate outcomes such as quality of life, fatigue, or clinical disease activity-free status, or they used measurement tools that differed from those planned in this review. In conclusion, compared to interferon beta-1a, alemtuzumab may improve relapse-free survival and sustained disease progression-free survival in individuals with relapsing-remitting MS over a 36-month period. It may have little to no impact on the proportion of participants experiencing at least one adverse event. However, the certainty of the evidence for these findings ranges from very low to low.
